record.title: CellAudit finds that predictive accuracy can mask unused intervention inputs
record.summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces CellAudit, a workflow that checks whether claimed model inputs are implemented in source code, affect fitted predictions, and improve prediction of observed responses. On BBBC047, the authors report an agent-selected model with held-out Global PCC 0.3153 that was invariant to compound replacement; a control-profile-only predictor scored 0.3142. Across 48 generated candidates, 47 changed under compound replacement, but only 20 showed positive target-loss gains on both held-out folds. Revisions recovered positive mean compound contributions. On an independently acquired cohort, dose-use evidence persisted while support for compound identity did not. These are detailed author-reported analyses, not an independent reproduction or proof of biological causality.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On BBBC047, the authors report an agent-selected predictor with held-out Global PCC 0.3153 that remained invariant to compound replacement, while a control-profile-only predictor scored 0.3142. They identify a blocked compound-query path and report that the invariance persisted after refitting with physically disjoint control wells for inputs and target references.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 48 generated candidates on two linked tasks, the authors report that 47 changed predictions under compound replacement on both held-out folds, but only 20 had target-loss gains with intervals above zero on both folds. Falsification-guided revisions recovered positive mean compound contributions on BBBC047.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a matched sci-Plex analysis, audit-enriched feedback had higher mean held-out prediction and larger mean compound and dose contributions across five paired trajectories, but paired intervals spanned zero. Refits on an independently acquired cohort retained dose contribution while support for compound identity did not persist.

evidence_gaps.description: The code-level input-path check, replacement tests and reported model-search outcomes have not been independently reproduced.

Input-use support depends on registered replacement distributions and is not evidence of biological exchangeability, mechanism or causal effects; compound-identity support did not persist in the reported LKCP transfer.

brief.importance_rationale: If the audit distinctions generalize, they could materially improve how agent-discovered biological predictors are evaluated by separating prediction from the claimed use and contribution of interventions. A 5 reflects a consequential evaluation method for AI-for-biology; the reported results remain specific to selected datasets, fitted models and registered replacement distributions.
limitations: All reported analyses are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.

The findings concern selected cellular-response datasets, fitted predictors and registered replacement distributions; a positive input contribution does not establish biological mechanism or causality.

The paper reports mixed evidence across measures: the sci-Plex paired intervals span zero, and support for compound identity fails to persist on the independently acquired LKCP cohort even though dose contribution persists.
Conclusions apply to the tested fits and checkpoints; evidence for one fit is not inherited by later refits.
The complete sci-Plex result evaluates an audit-enriched feedback package and does not isolate the effect of each diagnostic.
brief.summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces CellAudit, a workflow that checks whether claimed model inputs are implemented in source code, affect fitted predictions, and improve prediction of observed responses. On BBBC047, the authors report an agent-selected model with held-out Global PCC 0.3153 that was invariant to compound replacement; a control-profile-only predictor scored 0.3142. Across 48 generated candidates, 47 changed under compound replacement, but only 20 showed positive target-loss gains on both held-out folds. Revisions recovered positive mean compound contributions. technical.claimed_result: The authors report that held-out prediction can remain high while a registered intervention input is ignored; their audit distinguishes code-path access, fitted dependence and target-loss contribution, and uses falsification evidence to guide model revisions.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes the CellAudit workflow and reports results across BBBC047, linked perturbation tasks, sci-Plex and refits on an independently acquired cohort. All comparative outcomes remain author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed here.
technical.implementation_status: The paper links a project page. Its code, data and model checkpoints were not executed or independently audited in this activation.
technical.mechanism: CellAudit checks whether a registered input reaches the cited computation, replaces that input while holding other inputs and fitted checkpoints fixed to test prediction dependence, and measures whether the change improves target loss. It feeds source checks, grouped errors and contribution diagnostics into subsequent agent model search.
technical.regime: Agent-discovered cellular-response predictors using paired morphology/transcriptomics perturbation data; BBBC047 and related tasks, matched sci-Plex searches and fixed-design refits on LKCP. Findings depend on model, fold, cohort and registered input-replacement distribution.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint provides detailed splits, metrics, intervals and appendices, and links a project page. No independent code/data reproduction was performed in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: The control-profile-only predictor is the key BBBC047 reference; the paper also compares matched agent policies, fixed model designs and input-replacement tests across folds and cohorts.

brief.title: CellAudit finds that predictive accuracy can mask unused intervention inputs
brief.why_it_matters: A model can predict held-out cellular responses without using the intervention variable that its scientific claim says matters. Separating code-path use, fitted dependence and target-relevant contribution can expose that gap and guide revisions. The paper also shows that predictive transfer and input-use claims can diverge across cohorts. Its conclusions depend on registered replacement distributions and fitted model settings; they do not establish biological mechanism or causal effects.
